hints: Do not only look for C=C double bonds between carbons, look carefully at the oxygen atoms in these molecules too.
Remember that a carboxyl group (-COOH) has one C=O, and every peptide bond in a protein has one C=O, so count those as double bonds.
walkthrough:
**Remember what counts as a double bond**

Many students only think of C=C in lipids. In biology, C=O is also a double bond and it is everywhere.

Key examples: $C=C$ in unsaturated tails, $C=O$ in carboxyl groups and in peptide bonds.

**Check 1, the unsaturated fatty acid**

An unsaturated fatty acid has at least one $C=C$ in its hydrocarbon tail. It also has a carboxyl group at one end, which contains one $C=O$.

That is $1 + 1 = 2$ double bonds minimum, so 1 qualifies.

**Check 2 and 3, collagen and haemoglobin**

Both are proteins made of hundreds of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Every single peptide bond contains a $C=O$ double bond.

With hundreds of peptide bonds, they each contain far more than two double bonds. Haemoglobin also has extra double bonds in its four haem groups. So 2 and 3 both qualify, giving 1, 2 and 3.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. All three have at least two double bonds from C=C plus C=O in carboxyl and peptide bonds, plus haem in haemoglobin.
options.B: Misses out 3. Haemoglobin is a protein with hundreds of peptide bond C=O groups, so it easily has more than two double bonds.
options.C: Misses out 2. Collagen is a protein with hundreds of peptide bond C=O groups, so it easily has more than two double bonds.
options.D: Misses out 1. An unsaturated fatty acid has a C=C plus a C=O in its carboxyl group, so it has at least two double bonds.
